name: Umar Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Umar. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the big wheel loader at the Salt Flats lithium mine, an open pit out in the desert. My job is feeding the crusher, scooping the ore from the stockpile and dropping it into the hopper at a steady rate so the plant never runs dry or chokes. I'm on at five-thirty, check tyres and hydraulics, and then it's twelve hours of keeping that rhythm, plus covering for the other loader when it breaks down. I'm the one they call when the stockpile is a mess after a rain. The heat in January is brutal, and I love the moment the plant manager radios that we hit the daily tonnage.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My son Mateo and I run a small welding and fabrication workshop behind our house, mostly trailers, gates and farm repairs, on my days off. My wife Rosa does the books and keeps us honest. Our daughter Inés is a vet nurse in the city. I use AI every day, to price jobs, to check welding specs and to write the quotes, and I coach the junior soccer team on Saturdays when the workshop's quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a handy tool, nothing more, and anyone who said it'd change the world was selling something. I'd keep using it for quotes and specs. Online I'd post something like, work hard and use what helps, simple as that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my plan stays the same: work the loader to sixty-two or sixty-three, then go full-time in the workshop with Mateo. I'd be a little disappointed, because I like trying new things. But it's a safe picture for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and keep growing the workshop slowly, maybe one new customer a month. I'd use AI to cut my quoting time and keep the books neat for Rosa. And I'd keep putting a bit aside for the day I leave the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Steady as a full stockpile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a little disappointed. What did you hope for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a robot welder I could afford. The workshop can only take so much work with two pairs of hands. If AI made that cheaper, Mateo and I could take on twice the jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything in this picture that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lithium prices. They went up and down like a yo-yo the last few years. When they drop, they cut overtime, and that's real money for us.

S0.say: It's a handy tool, nothing more, and anyone who said it'd change the world was selling something. Work hard and use what helps, simple as that.
S0.think: My plan stays the same: work the loader to sixty-two or sixty-three, then go full-time in the workshop with Mateo. I'd be a little disappointed, but it's safe for us.
S0.do: Keeps doing his shifts and grows the workshop slowly, aiming for one new customer a month. Uses AI to cut quoting time and keeps saving for the day he leaves the mine.
S0.feel: Calm, steady as a full stockpile.
S0.quote: If AI made that cheaper, Mateo and I could take on twice the jobs.
S0.fieldNote: Umar thinks like a small business owner as much as a miner, and the plateau disappoints him because he hoped for cheaper automation. His plan centres on the family workshop with his son. Lithium price swings are his real background worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for people who are willing to work and learn. Businesses that adapt will do well, and the ones that wait will struggle. I'd say it at the soccer club and online, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for us. The mine might cut loader hours, but the workshop could grow if I can afford better tools. I'd be pushing to make the workshop our main income sooner than I planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a second-hand CNC plasma cutter for the workshop in the first year, around fifteen thousand dollars, using AI to learn the programs. I'd take on more farm and mine contract work with Mateo. And I'd keep my mine job for now, but I'd be ready to leave if they offered a decent package.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fifteen thousand is a big part of your savings. Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and Rosa would give me the look. But I've done the numbers, and if it brings in three new jobs a month, it pays for itself in a year. I'd rather bet on my own business than leave the money sitting in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the mine would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young loader operators who don't have a trade behind them. I'd offer a couple of them weekend work in the workshop so they learn welding. That's how my uncle taught me.

S1.say: This is a chance for people willing to work and learn. Businesses that adapt will do well, and the ones that wait will struggle.
S1.think: I think it's good for us: the mine might cut loader hours, but the workshop could grow with better tools. I'd push to make it our main income sooner than planned.
S1.do: Buys a second-hand CNC plasma cutter for about fifteen thousand dollars in the first year and learns it with AI. Takes on more contract work with his son and stays at the mine while ready to take a good package.
S1.quote: I'd rather bet on my own business than leave the money sitting in the bank.
S1.fieldNote: Umar sees steady change as a business opportunity and would put a large share of his savings into the workshop. He trusts his own numbers and enterprise more than a bank balance. His instinct to help young operators is through apprenticeship-style weekend work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to be rough, and people will need to stick together, families and communities especially. I don't want the government running everything, but I'd accept they need to help in a crisis like this. I'd say that at the club and at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, if robots can do my loader job and welding too, the workshop isn't safe either. I'd be sixty in 2028 with a few months' savings and a son whose future depends on our little business. That keeps me up more than my own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first package from the mine and put part of it into a welding robot for the workshop, so we're the ones using the robots, not competing with them. I'd chase every contract repairing and modifying the new automated machines while they still need people. And Rosa and I would cut back hard at home to keep a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not lost, but running fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a robot when robots are the problem. Talk me through that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If every shop has robot welders in two years, the only shops left are the ones that bought them first. I'd rather own the robot than be beaten by someone who does. It's the same as buying the first plasma cutter in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mateo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him the workshop is still ours, but it'll look different. He'd have to learn to program and fix the robots, not just weld. And I'd tell him I'm sorry it came so fast, because I wanted to hand him something steady.

S2.say: This is going to be rough, and families and communities will need to stick together. I don't want government running everything, but they need to help in a crisis like this.
S2.think: If robots can do my loader job and welding too, the workshop isn't safe either. I'd be sixty with a few months' savings and a son whose future depends on our little business, and that keeps me up.
S2.do: Takes the first mine package and puts part of it into a welding robot for the workshop. Chases contract work repairing and modifying the new automated machines and cuts back hard at home.
S2.feel: Anxious, not lost but running fast.
S2.quote: I'd rather own the robot than be beaten by someone who does.
S2.fieldNote: Umar's response to fast AGI is to buy into the automation himself rather than resist it. His real worry is his son, whose future he tied to the workshop. He softens his free-market stance enough to accept that government must help in a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for people to plan if they're willing to put the work in. Businesses should adapt, families should help each other, and the government should mostly stay out of the way. That's what I'd tell anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to make the workshop strong before the mine job ends. I'd leave the mine at sixty-one, in 2029, and go full-time with Mateo. By 2031, we'd be the shop that knows how to fix the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd buy the plasma cutter, then save for a welding robot by 2029. I'd do online courses on robot maintenance at night, with AI helping me study. And I'd plan my exit from the mine for 2029, so I leave with my pride and a good reference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is it different from 2028 for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028, I'm grabbing whatever I can. In 2031, I can build a proper business plan, show Mateo the numbers and get the bank on side. It's the difference between a fire sale and a launch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you hire anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, maybe one of the young loader operators from the mine who wants to learn. I'd train him the old way, side by side. That's better than any handout.

S3.say: Five years is enough time for people willing to put the work in. Businesses should adapt, families should help each other, and the government should mostly stay out of the way.
S3.think: Five years is enough to make the workshop strong before the mine job ends. I'd leave the mine at sixty-one in 2029 and go full-time with Mateo, and by 2031 we'd be the shop that fixes robots.
S3.do: Buys the plasma cutter in year one and saves for a welding robot by 2029. Studies robot maintenance online at night with AI and plans to leave the mine in 2029 to run the workshop full-time.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but more excited than worried.
S3.quote: It's the difference between a fire sale and a launch.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Umar's scramble into a business plan, and he relishes it. He would leave the mine early by choice to build the workshop with his son. His values show in wanting to train a young worker side by side rather than rely on handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so get busy. Learn a trade, start something, look after your family. Nobody's going to hand you a future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's a good picture. I'd leave the mine around sixty-two and build the workshop into something Mateo can run for decades. The robots would be our tools by then, not our competition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the loader for now and expand the workshop step by step: the plasma cutter next year, a welding robot in four or five years. I'd keep using AI for quoting, design and learning. And I'd set up the workshop as a proper family company with Mateo as a partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite hopeful, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about it bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young ones who don't have a family business to fall back on. Not every kid has a dad with a workshop. I'd want the schools to bring back proper trades classes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Inés?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's a vet nurse, and I'd guess people want a human hand on their dog for a long while yet. I'd tell her to keep learning and save. And that there's always a bench for her in the workshop if she ever wants one, though she hates welding.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift, so get busy: learn a trade, start something, look after your family. Nobody's going to hand you a future.
S4.think: For me it's a good picture. I'd leave the mine around sixty-two and build the workshop into something Mateo can run for decades, with robots as our tools, not our competition.
S4.do: Keeps working the loader while expanding the workshop step by step, with a plasma cutter next year and a welding robot in four or five years. Uses AI for quoting and design and makes his son a partner in a family company.
S4.quote: Not every kid has a dad with a workshop.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Umar sees nothing but opportunity for his family business. His concern is for young people without a family trade to fall back on, and he wants trades classes back in schools. His entrepreneurial streak runs through every answer, consistent with his free-market views.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time to build the workshop before both the mine job and the welding work get hit. What would help is easy small-business loans for people buying their own automation, and trades training in schools so young people have something to stand on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what the robots will need. Every machine breaks, gets bent, needs a bracket made or a part modified. Somebody local with a welder and a brain will be in demand longer than people think.

headlineQuote: Somebody local with a welder and a brain will be in demand longer than people think.
portrait: Umar Alvarez is a 58-year-old wheel loader operator at an open-pit lithium mine who also runs a welding and fabrication workshop with his son and uses AI every day. He believes in hard work, family enterprise and free markets, and sees most change as a business opportunity. He is calm under the plateau and steady change, plans to buy his own automation, and only becomes anxious with AGI in 2028, mainly for his son's future. With five or ten years he plans to leave the mine early and build the workshop into a family company that fixes robots.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there would be no time to build the workshop before both his mine job and the welding work are hit.
whatWouldHelp: Easy small-business loans for people buying their own automation, and trades training in schools.
